title: University of Leeds Research with BNCA Explores Sustainable Cooling for Heat-Vulnerable Communities in Pune
summary: University of Leeds researchers, with BNCA and Barefoot Story, are working with Pune's informal settlements to develop sustainable, inclusive cooling solutions.
body_html:
Pune, 16 November 2026: Researchers from the University of Leeds are working with partners in India to understand how chronic urban heat affects marginalised communities in Pune and to identify sustainable cooling solutions that can help them adapt to rising temperatures.

The project brings together the University of Leeds, Dr Bhanuben Nanavati College of Architecture (BNCA), a women's higher education institution in Pune, and Barefoot Story, a social enterprise working in architecture, interiors and urban design. It focuses on residents of informal settlements, who face greater exposure to extreme heat because of limited access to cooling technologies, reliable infrastructure and green spaces, as well as overcrowded housing and outdoor working conditions.

The team is working with residents of Kishkindha Nagar and Shinde Vasti settlements to learn how they experience heat stress, how they cope and what solutions they would like to see. Dr Catherine Bale, Associate Professor of Sustainable Urban Energy Systems at the School of Earth, Environment and Sustainability, University of Leeds, said, “Rising temperatures are a big issue. Pune used to be considered to have a comfortable climate. Now it is becoming very uncomfortable with chronic heat stress and prolonged, hotter summers.” She noted that around 40% of the city's population live in informal settlements.

The research uses participatory systems mapping, which brings residents and other stakeholders together to build a full picture of the city's existing cooling landscape and to help municipal policymakers see how decisions in one area can affect outcomes across the city. Sumedha Basu, Postdoctoral Researcher at the University of Leeds, said, “Rather than treating residents as participants, we recognised them as key knowledge holders whose lived experience is essential for understanding the challenges posed by extreme heat. We found that heat had become much more intolerable for them.” She said policy makers need to integrate a heat action plan with sustainable cooling plans, adding, “For example, citizens want cool roofs, community cooling centres and retrofitting of homes to increase long-term heat resilience for the most vulnerable.”

The project has also produced resources for local communities, including educational playing cards and a video in Marathi, to help residents understand climate adaptation and take part in discussions on local cooling strategies.

BNCA helped establish the network of residents and city stakeholders, while Barefoot Story co-produced research insights and played a key role in fieldwork. Namrata Dhamanakar, Professor at the Department of Environmental Architecture and Planning (DEAP) at BNCA, said, “Through post-occupancy evaluation studies and field-based data collection, we worked closely with residents to understand how heat affects their homes, health and everyday lives.” Mandar Athavale, Assistant Professor at BNCA and Co-founder of Barefoot Story, said, “Most research on heat and health in informal settlements rests on secondary data. This project begins an enquiry from the ground up, gathering residents' own accounts of how heat affects their health and daily lives.”

The researchers say the findings from Pune could offer insights for cities in both developed and developing countries. Dr Bale said, “We can draw on lessons learned in India to examine how communities can respond to rising temperatures while reducing energy use and carbon emissions.”
